Furthermore, we explore how environmental policies and technological advancements affect the economics of emergency spinning reserves, providing valuable insights for policymakers navigating this complex issue.

Consider a function f made up of the composition of the following basic functions: polynomial, exponential, and logarithm. Since f is part of a composite function, it must be elementarily expressible in terms of 1/x, x, e^x, and log(x). Notably, f can be an expression involving 1/x. The purpose of this study is to determine the overall structure of its n-th iterated form when applied to a rational function.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production at the LHC, we have been analyzing the matrix element for four particles (HH to b b W W*) and connecting it to the effective field theory framework. Specifically, we are investigating the impact of considering the HH system as a single entity versus treating it as two individual Higgs bosons. This comparison involves examining the accuracy of the effective field theory description in terms of its operator coefficients. To this end, we have been analyzing the differential cross section for non-resonant Higgs pair production in a specific channel (b b W W*) and evaluating the matrix element method's effectiveness. This analysis shines light on the HH system's internal dynamics and is relevant for future LHC experiments that will deeply probe this process.

We investigate how precision research in $e^+ e^-\to Zh$ and $e^+ e^-\to \gamma \gamma$ processes can help shed light on the extended scalar sector of the Standard Model. Taking into account the effects of operator mixing and utilizing a multi-parameter approach, we show that certain current and future $e^+ e^-\to \gamma \gamma$ data or facility capabilities such as CLIC or ILC could significantly reveal first-generation multi-SM scalar interactions. Furthermore, $e^+ e^-\to Zh$ research at FFAG, CLIC, ILC, or future HEP facilities or even energy fringes of $e^+ e^-\to \gamma \gamma$ research could provide crucial insights or complementary constraints on second-generation multi-SM scalar interactions. We also find that $e^+ e^-\to Zh$ research is more sensitive to many parameters than $e^+ e^-\to \gamma \gamma$, with in some cases, the sensitivity up to five to ten times greater.

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by strong and permanent weather patterns,  surrounded by circular features that represent the boundary between which temperature and wind patterns significantly change.  Observations from the Cassini spacecraft reveal that, in the northern hemisphere, a polar vortex forms every eight and a half Earth years in the region that will soon experience summer.  This particular vortex was found to be surrounded by a temperature gradient that forms a hexagonal shape, unlike the circular boundary typically seen around the southern hemisphere's vortex.  The formation of this vortex in the northern hemisphere is expected to follow a particular sequence of seasonal changes, and its formation may be related to the temperature gradient that forms a hexagonal shape around it.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, within a bounded, convex domain formed by the intersection of two analytic surfaces in R^3. We demonstrate that solutions which do not change sign and are defined on a time interval doubling its initial length will eventually become defined on a quadruply extended time interval, under the condition that certain compactness or a nontrivial symmetry phenomenon apply. This analysis allows us to establish the existence of locally defined explosion solutions.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric analyses for varieties defined by polynomial equations with coefficients from a finite set of rational numbers can be carried out in a way that is universally accurate for all positive characteristic numbers.

The manner in which the surface of bimetallic compounds is terminated has a significant effect on the metallic vs nonmetallic behavior observed in ultrathin V$_2$O$_3$ layers.  Our analysis of combined core and valence photoemission spectra using LEED and STM reveals that oxygen-terminating the V$_2$O$_3$(0001) surface produces a nonmetallic state in V$_2$O$_3$ layers just one layer thick despite being close to a ferromagnetic metal in its bulk form.  This result is attributed to changes in oxygen bonding that cause a significant charge transfer from the V$^{3+}$ layer to the oxygen layer, counteracting the spontaneous ferromagnetism inherent in V$_2$O$_3$.  In contrast, oxygen-terminating double layers and smaller thicknesses exhibit metal-insulator shifts that are not as well understood.  Alternatively, oxygen-terminating single layer thicknesses may also be the result of a specific surface termination-induced defect structure found only in this depth.  Notably, terminating V$_2$O$_3$(0001) with vanadium produces a metallic state in both single and double layer thicknesses, and this may be attributed to lower density surface oxygen defects as well as V$^{2+}$ ions that act as hole carriers when the film is thin enough and there is not enough energy to localize the charge over an entire layer.

Our paper investigates the quantum double dark-rogue wave state, which represents an isolated system of two colliding Bose-Einstein condensates with different quantum properties. We examine the physical states of this system at specific times during the collision and in different regions. In particular, we measure the ratio of particles in each condensate as the collision progresses. This ratio follows a consistent pattern, regardless of the initial state or how it was created. We relate this pattern to a specific function that describes the average distribution of particles and use it to predict how a notepad-like state behaves. Furthermore, we define a critical moment when the system's behavior starts to differ significantly and use this to create a precise formula for how Bose-Einstein condensation forms in larger, more complex systems.

We introduce a novel property called 'polarization' in the context of structured collections, identifying a symmetry in these structures that leads to a transformation into a more manageable forms - specifically, a transformation into a collection that is easily computable and stable. This polarization process, applicable to systems defined by differential equations and inequalities, is a contraction that yields distinct results for forward and backward directions. As a result, we can distinguish left- and right-handed versions of any structure. This concept of polarization was first mentioned by Ilyashenko, and we demonstrate its connection to the polarization phenomenon in differential equations, revealing a link to symmetric solutions and wrapping areas. We also explore methods for identifying polarized collections and discuss potential connections to other concepts, such as symmetries and dualities.

This informal note begins by illustrating a technical example related to GSH's work on mod $p$ representation of GL_n(A_K) in the paper "Irreducible A_f-slices for complex GL_n". The discussion then veers off topic to explore the relationship between harmonic analysis and measure theory on reductive adelic groups. The write also mentions his ongoing project with A. Touati on reductive group orbital integrals.

Performing experimental measurements on nuclear time-dependent behavior remains a significant challenge for nuclear physics. The study of neutron-star mergers and asymmetric collisions demands the development of new experimental techniques to understand nuclear reconstruction in extreme conditions. Resonant x-ray scattering offers a promising approach to study nuclear reconstruction, by using x-ray pulses to monitor the interaction between x-rays and nuclear matter in laboratory settings. Specifically, researchers propose using x-ray diffusion to measure the time it takes for x-rays to pass through a target nuclear material, located in front of a resonant absorber. This method involves determining the time it takes for x-rays to shift from transparent to opaque, and has been demonstrated capable of detecting small changes in density associated with nuclear reconstruction over multiple orders of magnitude. Researchers also examine alternative methods, including interferometry, and find that resonant x-ray diffusion provides the most robust and accurate measurement of nuclear reconstruction, out of the methods considered.

We investigate the stability of quantum error correction circuits using a classical Ising model on a cubic lattice, incorporating both nearest-neighbor interactions and self-interactions for each spin. By analyzing the effective interaction strengths in the classical model, which are influenced by the quantum error correction circuit's propagation times and coupling strengths, we identify a wide range of stable operating conditions for the quantum system. These findings suggest that deeply entangled quantum states, such as the 2D toric code, can be made robust against local noise with moderate self-interactions. Additionally, our results demonstrate that strongly coupled spins can significantly increase the stability of these quantum states. To validate these predictions, we perform a classical Monte Carlo simulation to calculate the decay rates of the quantum system's boundary degrees of freedom and find that they match the predictions from a linearized stability analysis.

Recent theoretical predictions stating that group VI elemental monolayers can't be in the form of a honeycomb lattice structure have been disputed by new experimental findings. In this study, it's been found that incorporating oxygen into these monolayers, specifically tellurene, makes them dynamically stable and topologically non-trivial in the form of a honeycomb lattice. Oxygen functionalization brings about unique filtering effects on the orbits, breaks spatial symmetry, and produces the desired exotic quantum properties. A key characteristic of this system is its large-gap of around 0.36 eV, alongside isolated Dirac cones on the edges which indicate potential applications for room temperature spin-transport. Investigations of the spin Hall conductivity and berry curvatures show high conductivity when compared to other Xene materials. These properties can be quantified with the Z2 invariant and Chern number both being 1. A practical implementation of this is demonstrated in strain engineered hBN/TeO/hBN quantum wells that exhibit a significant non-trivial gap of 0.11 eV. Oxygen functionalization brings robust and stable electronic properties that could facilitate efficient spin orbit coulomb interactions for the TeO monolayer, making it feasible to manufacture this material using chemical functionalization rather than exploring less likely solutions of strain or magic crystal growth.

We have developed a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous medium. This method combines traditional finite element and boundary element techniques, leveraging the R-T and M-P formulations to model frictionless contact between parallel cracks. By incorporating the boundary element approach for the Darcy flow problem, we obtained a consolidated weak formulation that can be solved using a hybrid-mixed finite element and boundary element strategy. Our proposed method exceeds the accuracy of the R-T formulation and is more efficient than the M-P approach, especially in scenarios with highly conducting fractures. To evaluate our method's effectiveness, we applied it to all possible hybrid-mixed finite element configurations, including those that have not been extensively tested, and observed that it yields significant improvements in accuracy. Furthermore, we observed that our method can produce negative node pressures, which may be mitigated by implementing a limiting technique. Our method also introduces an additional degree of freedom associated with the crack function, but this can be minimized by solving a system of size three. We are currently exploring ways to extend this method to multiple conducting fractures and the flow of multiple phases within a single conducting fracture.

A critical challenge in developing spin-based electronic devices is the difficulty in controlling spin orientation due to various forms of decoherence. To overcome this limitation, researchers are exploring the potential of superconducting systems to reduce decoherence and maintain spin orientation through rigorous pairing. In these systems, the spin of particles is inherently locked to the direction of superconducting pair moment, enabling reliable transmission of information encoded in spin orientation. In this study, the proposal of a spin switch is presented, which leverages the unique properties of a superconducting layer combined with a helical magnetic layer to achieve this control over spin orientation. The proposed device design involves a point contact or a quantum dot located at the interface between these two components. When a small magnetic field is applied perpendicular to the helical magnetic layer, a significant effect is observed on the pair moment's direction, resulting in a substantial modification of spin exchange and local magnetic fields. Consequently, this causes a significant shift in the density of states at the point contact or the resonance state of the quantum dot, ultimately leading to a significant alteration in electric resistance. This proposes a superconducting spin switch capable of reliably transmitting information encoded in spin orientation.

The recent resurgence of Bayesian methods has led to the development of several novel models, bayes factors, and model-averaged estimates. While these methods are now widely known, a full integration into mainstream statistical practice has yet to be achieved. One major obstacle is the lengthy computation time required for Bayesian analysis, which is typically addressed through the use of approximations such as Laplace approximations or Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) simulations. However, researchers have thus far overlooked the potential benefits of these methods due to their limited precision and reliability. In this paper, we propose a range of computational workflows that leverage these methods, focusing on nested designs in which the comparison of research studies involves the meta-analysis of individual data sets. Our workflow framework allows for the incorporation of study characteristics into analysis choices, such as the selection of models and the application of priors. This framework also enables researchers to conduct reliable and fast Bayesian analysis by utilizing recent developments in computational algorithms, such as the advent of scalable Monte Carlo methods that bypass the need for MCMC simulations. The use of Bayesian meta-analysis, in particular, allows researchers to obtain accurate estimates, make informed decisions, and conduct rigorous posterior model validation using modern techniques and computational resources.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To date, research on these indicators has focused on their role in connecting sentences, but without accounting for the underlying semantics. This semantic aspect is crucial in managing complex information within models and in predicting subtle pattern variations. To address this gap, we present a novel, specially designed dataset called DiscSense, which collects information about the semantic relationships between sentences that contain certain discourse indicators. This dataset encompasses 15 categories of discourse indicators and almost 16,000 labeled instances in seven languages. To thoroughly examine the properties of discourse indicators, we have undertaken extensive, language-specific analysis using the DiscSense dataset. This analysis involves conducting automated tests to compare the semantics of sentences connected by different indicators, as well as analyzing how the meaning of these sentences varies based on factors such as the connected clause's location and the presence of punctuation. To achieve this, we have developed an empirical method that is applicable across multiple languages and can be applied to any dataset labeled with discourse indicators. This approach is versatile and can be applied to various discourse indicators as well as to the analysis of punctuation in connected clauses.

We investigate the properties of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond under high-temperature conditions, examining their behavior at 700 nanometers and across various temperature ranges. Uncovered are the thermal dissociation of paired nitrogen atoms surrounding the NV center and temperature limitations due to thermal diffusion and heating methods. By utilizing a heat-bath technique, we are able to accurately regulate temperature and observe the NV center's spectral characteristics at 90 Kelvin, 300 Kelvin, and temperatures in between. Our findings include the identification of multiple spectral lines, confirming that the NV center retains its spin properties even when surrounded by multiple nitrogen atoms, as well as the detection of pairs with various separations. The results of our research provide a foundation for using NV centers in diamond under high-temperature conditions and offer insights into potential applications such as diamond-based thermometry.

The underlying mechanisms of cortical circuits remain somewhat enigmatic despite the substantial advances made in recent years. In this study, we propose a novel neural network based on the principles of brain biology. This model is unique in its ability to efficiently learn and generalize to new tasks while also maintaining excellent performance in tasks that require quick action, as evidenced by its superiority in multiple benchmarks. We contend that this neural network and its associated training regimen accurately capture the essential functions of the brain's learning and training processes.

Using field-theoretic methods, researchers studied a quantum spin model based on the SU(3) representation on a triangular lattice, finding that its ground state is an antiferromagnetic moment for lattice spacings smaller than a critical value. To gain a deeper understanding, they mapped the model to a sigma model and evaluated its topological term, demonstrating that it corresponds to a parity-breaking term that is relevant in the model's low-density regime. By incorporating the external magnetic field into the sigma model, they found that it leads to an unstable point at zero magnetic field, which determines the phase structure of the model. Furthermore, they established that the model's low-density regime is characterized by chiral magnetrically ordered states, and that these states can be reached experimentally.

In this study, we establish a new computational framework based on B-spline basis functions for solving the Hartree-Fock problem using a finite basis set method. This framework's core aspect is an efficient algorithm for determining the overlap and integration matrices needed to calculate the Hartree-Fock equations. We demonstrate the accuracy of our method by applying it to a simple electron gas model, as well as hydrogen atoms and clusters, and find that it yields precise results comparable to conventional finite basis set methods. Additionally, we analyze the time and computational cost requirements for our method, showing that it achieves significant speed-ups, particularly with more advanced central potential models. To facilitate adoption, a free software program called Bsplinhf has been developed and is available for download, allowing users to execute the B-spline Hartree-Fock technique on various central potential models.

The concept of synchronization among oscillators in various systems has been extensively explored, yet the conditions for explosive synchronization, which occurs when a small number of tightly coupled oscillators rapidly synchronize a larger, less coupled population, are not well understood. We present a novel, universally applicable standard for measuring explosive synchronization in populations of oscillators subject to different coupling schemes, establishing a clear distinction between explosive and gradual synchronization. Through extensive simulations of three distinct oscillator models in one and two dimensions, our results consistently demonstrate that explosive synchronization arises when the population's overall synchronization rate is significantly higher than its disconnection rate, especially in regions where the population can connect externally. These findings hold substantial implications for the development of more precise models and the control of self-organizing systems in complexity networks.

We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed rank and orthogonality constraint, and demonstrate that under specific conditions, its landscape is globally optimizable from a particular Riemannian perspective. To achieve this, we first present a novel analysis of a nonconvex matrix decomposition problem with orthogonal constraints, and establish that it yields a globally optimizable problem in a particular Riemannian manifold. Our approach is based on an in-depth examination of the Riemannian Hessian from a geodesic perspective, and determines the extragradient algorithm as a critical component for achieving global optimality. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the optimal solutions in the geodesic and Euclidean contexts. Our results are highly relevant to three-specific applications: low-rank representation in signal processing, matrix factorization, and independent component analysis.

A signless version of a classic theorem from graph theory has been presented in a counterexample: there exists a cubic bipartite graph that cannot be colored using an odd number of colors, making it impossible to achieve a tractable upper bound for a specific chromatic number when using a certain algorithm.

Let $q\ge 3$ be an integer, with $\chi$ denoting a Dirichlet character modulo $q$ and $L(s,\chi)$ being the associated Dirichlet L-functions. This paper will present specific function series, along with their identities, linking them to $L$-functions for real s values greater than 1.

High-energy particles with mass up to $10^{19}$ GeV, possibly associated with the origin of primordial fields, may influence Particle Physics and the Early Universe through their decay. These particles could have sizes comparable to the gravitational wavelength of primordial fluctuations ($\sim 10^6$ m) due to an underlying theory's symmetry restrictions. As a result, their interaction with ordinary matter is mediated over large distances, leading to unique observational effects that may link particle physics with the structure of the Universe. The proposed Beyond-Standard-Model (BSM) framework "Cosmic Threads" explores the implications of these particles on the Universe's evolution and their accessible signatures in cosmic rays, the sky, and particle physics experiments.

Our experiments examine how the geometric structure of force-free swimmers interacts with different types of fluid friction. We focused on swimmers with rigid bodies made of different shapes, including cylinders, squares and triangles, and observed that those with asymmetrical front and back areas moved more efficiently in a non-freezing fluid when pushed by a steady flow of fluid. This occurred because asymmetrical swimmers can maintain a steady helical motion by changing the angle of their axis. Our findings show that this axis angle controls the swimmer's speed and can be influenced by the fluid's friction. However, the type of fluid friction doesn't affect the swimmer's ability to move its axis angle. We also found that some asymmetrical swimmers can move their axis angle to a position that reduces friction, resulting in higher speeds in a stationary fluid. Our research provides evidence that swimmers with irregular shapes that can move their internal parts can move more efficiently in a non-freezing fluid when pushed by a steady flow of fluid, and that their speed is controlled by how these internal parts are shaped.

We examined the evolution of Nash Equilibrium in a repeated Cournot game among three rival firms, using a co-evolutionary genetic approach in a simulated environment. Our study was conducted over various parameter settings, and through multiple trial runs, we obtained significant evidence for the emergence of a Nash Equilibrium solution through the co-evolutionary genetic process. This solution was consistently observed across different simulation runs, as validated by the p-value < 0.008, thus supporting our hypothesis. Furthermore, our analysis highlighted the importance of the co-evolutionary genetic model in achieving a Nash Equilibrium solution by conducting a comparison with an evolutionary genetic approach, resulting in a success rate of 0.266 in the Cournot game scenario.

The growing complexity of modern knowledge graphs necessitates the use of advanced techniques to enhance them through the analysis of unstructured text. Machine learning methods can be particularly useful for this purpose, as they allow for the automatic identification and addition of high-quality factual information to a knowledge base formatted as an ontology. In this research, we propose a novel approach based on deep learning, which incorporates entity recognition, relationship recognition, and ontological enhancement modules to add new entities and relationships to an existing ontology, while avoiding existing duplicates. The proposed approach includes two primary components. Firstly, a pre-trained entity recognizer is used to identify entities within a given text, their relationships, and their classifications, as defined in an existing ontology. Secondly, a relationship validator is employed to filter out inappropriate relationships, prioritize likely ones, and merge overlapping relationships. The proposed approach was tested on NLM Senses, a sense annotation dataset, and Wikipedia, a vast knowledge base.

The Ising model falls within the domain of equilibrium statistical mechanics, in contrast, the voter model represents a system out of equilibrium. Our study examines an extended model that combines Ising and voter agents on a fully connected graph, and we derive exact expressions for its stationary state. Furthermore, we analyze the model's dynamics in a sector of balanced configurations and demonstrate that it is effectively isolated from the equilibrium Ising model. The model's behavior in this balanced sector is more complex than its counterpart in the complete graph Ising model, which is instead influenced by the model's dynamics in a sector of uniformly aligned configurations.

This investigation focuses on understanding how airborne viruses are spread through population groups, particularly as weather conditions fluctuate. The model developed considers various weather patterns, including tropical, temperate, and arctic environments. The model shows that extreme temperature changes and low wind speeds in arctic climates slow virus dissemination, while tropical climates facilitate spread. In temperate climates, dissemination accelerates in autumn. The model indicates that a significant drop in spread occurs at low wind speeds in all climates. The study finds that arctic climates inhibit dissemination below a certain wind speed threshold, while tropical and temperate climates show a broader sensitivity in dissemination.

Deep learning models hold significant potential for exploring complex systems and predicting unknown quantities, but the inherent flaws in their construction and the limitations of their testing data introduce irrevocable uncertainties, ultimately affecting their predictive capability. The scope of this study expands on the earlier work mentioned in reference [1] to also encompass models that utilize data from multiple sources, incorporating differences in data quality, of which users wish to know about the uncertainties associated with their predictions. The research presents several new techniques for evaluating the uncertainties of these predictions, as well as comparisons between them, which are conducted across multiple types of models, datasets, and prediction tasks. The findings of this research, which include the development of a publicly accessible framework for conducting similar experiments, provide insights that are relevant to any application involving the prediction of continuous outcomes with uncertain meanings.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and normal powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$ have the same property of containing a given ideal $I$. This applies to instances where $I$ is a prime ideal with a specific height. The normal and symbolic powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$ were shown in a previous work to always contain the symbolic and normal powers of the ordinary power series ring $k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$. Here, we prove that this inheritance holds only in cases where $I$ is a prime ideal with a specific height. Additionally, we provide a condition which ensures that a given prime ideal with a specific height is contained in the normal or symbolic powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$. This condition is based on the relationship between the weights of the vertices in $\mathcal{D}$ and the height of the ideal $I$.

We've established a new representation for the partition function in an O(N) invariant quantum matrix model, using a finite N approach. This partition function is expressed as a sum over divided difference operators acting on a set of basis functions, characterized by interlacing eigenvalue spectra. These basis functions are related to Schur polynomials, which are organized according to the irreducible representations of the symmetric group $S_N$. Notably, this partition function is linked to the interparticle correlations in a quantum harmonic oscillator system. Our analysis reveals a conserved quantity in this finite N system, enabling us to derive an exact expression for the partition function using the geometric series. This approach is shown to be equivalent to a brute force computation using the divided difference operators.

Convolutional neural networks are integral to various image scanning technology, including infrared, radar, and sonar systems. Their reliability is crucial, yet they are prone to degradation from harsh environmental conditions and hardware flaws. Traditional security measures for these networks typically focus on external threats, neglecting the impact of hardware defects on their performance. We propose a novel approach to detect and contain the effect of hardware faults on CNNs by analyzing the patterns of their activation functions. Unlike existing fault detection methods that utilize entire network outputs or weight datasets, our approach only requires access to activation interval information. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method through practical implementations and performance assessments on multiple datasets.

The government's method of allocating settlement duties is influenced by a collaboration of firms that operate within the financial sector, including banks and insurance companies. The proposed algorithm for determining settlement obligations is based on the general principle of equal treatment, ensuring that firms with similar capabilities are held to the same standard. The proposed method is compared to an existing approach, specifically the Romanian Ministry of Finance's algorithm, by utilizing actual data from the Romanian financial sector. The comparison shows the proposed algorithm yields more equitable results, whereas the existing approach produces biased outcomes.

This paper establishes a one-parameter subgroup of transformations based on the Jordanian twist, thereby extending the work by Khare, Daugherty, and Hakova. Building upon this, we derive explicit expressions for the corresponding Lie algebra element and determine its non-trivial central and annihilation extensions. Additionally, we obtain a second-order differential equation characterizing the one-parameter subalgebras, and we demonstrate that the 9-dimensional solvable Lie algebras of type A, encompassing subalgebras like g_43 and g_13, can be categorized based on this differential equation. Furthermore, we investigate the 2-step nilpotent Lie algegs' one-parameter subalgebras and demonstrate the equivalence between the twisted Lie algebra approach and the method involving twisted coordinates, providing a differential equation that 2-step nilpotent Lie algebras must satisfy.

Constructing a rich semantic space for multiple languages is the foundation for successful cross-lingual natural language understanding. Current methods represent words in each language as corresponding vectors, with the goal of mapping these vectors into a common high-dimensional space. Although some methods have achieved significant success in tasks like word translation and few-shot learning, they often overlook the organization of words within each language. In contrast, our proposed approach, Cluster-consistent Multi-lingual Word Representation, incorporates the organizational structure of words within each language, building on the concept of distributed representations and cluster-preserving projections. We establish a new model that learns multi-lingual word representations while maintaining the intrinsic relationships between words in each language. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through experiments on low-resource language classification, where we achieve notable improvements over baseline models and surpass the performance of cross-lingual learning methods.

The study provides first-time data on the creation of pions, kaons, protons and $\phi$ mesons during Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV. The research offers fresh insights into particle production in heavy-ion collisions, building on existing LHC data, and establishes initial conditions for relativistic hydrodynamics in Xe-Xe collisions. Created particle yields can vary based on centralities and medium properties, which are derived from beam energy and number of quark gluon plasma participants. The research reveals that the ratio of kaon and proton production remains consistent with quark fragmentation ratios, while the ratio of pion to proton production and the proton temperature remain consistent with quark fragmentation and thermal models, respectively. The research also provides first-time data on the creation of $\phi$ mesons in heavy-ion collisions and finds that $\phi$ meson creation is similar to that of protons, which is in line with the suggestion that protons originate from the decay of heavy mesons.

The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable errors in its labels. These flaws hinder the development of high-percentage accurate systems. To address this challenge, we present the ASSIST dataset, a refined version of MultiWOZ 2.0 with corrected labels and introduces the problem of building robust dialogue state tracking systems in the presence of label imperfections. Additionally, we introduce a new evaluation metric called K-Split ratio to assess the performance of models when testing on unseen labels. Through various experiments, our proposed framework achieves notable improvements in accuracy and demonstrates the benefits of using weak supervision when testing on unseen data.

In late October 2019, widespread protests erupted in Chile, resulting in both peaceful and violent gatherings that spread rapidly across the country. Using epidemiological methods, we developed a theoretical model to simulate the spread of protests in this context. Our approach accounts for non-local connection effects among individuals and varies the likelihood of violent behavior based on the distance between people's locations. By incorporating these factors, our model accurately predicts the regional protest intensity gradients observed in Chile during this time period. Our analysis highlights the significant impact of pre-protest social conditions and physical connectivity on the likelihood of violent gatherings, as well as the critical role of connectedness in shaping the spread of protests globally. Furthermore, we facilitate access to our epidemiological simulation model through a publicly available online platform, allowing users to explore and visualize the dynamics of the protests through interactive visualizations and simulations.

By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features do not align with observations, we find that the accuracy of the predictions for the brackett-gamma line is a useful indicator of the overall validity of the model's star formation rate estimation.

We are studying a critical boundary that involves breaking down real polynomials into the sum of squares of other real polynomials, specifically those that don't equal zero. This specific boundary overlaps with another critical boundary that involves nonnegative polynomials and is characterized by polynomials that become zero at at least one point. Our focus lies on a separate part of the boundary that involves positive polynomials and we have already successfully identified the complete description for some specific cases with low degrees in a small number of variables. However, more complex cases with more variables or higher degree polynomials remain to be fully understood and there is currently very limited knowledge on them. Using an assumption from D. Eisenbud, M. Green, and J. Harris, we have obtained new restrictions for the number of decomposed polynomials and the matrix dimensions in this context. These new restrictions particularly improve our understanding for homogeneous quartic polynomials in 5 variables and they match a recent confirmed case in this context. Lastly, combining both theoretical calculations and computational techniques, we have obtained specific examples and counterexamples to further analyze the general applicability of G. Blekherman's findings and we have proven that the established bounds are indeed reachable.

In high-scale theories involving extra neutrino states, the standard low-energy matrix used to describe neutrino interactions may be invalid. We reevaluate how much is currently known about individual components of this matrix, making no assumption about its unitarity. We establish two fundamental sets of experimental limitations - direct plus inherent constraints, and indirect ones. We examine the effects of each set on the possible deviation of neutrino behavior from expected unitarity. We also provide a clearer understanding of predictions related to flux and cross-sections, taking into consideration any contamination from new physics affecting hadronic measurements. We focus on the currently operating FASER$\nu$ experiment to show that certain neutrino experiments have sensitivity to this issue. We discovered that certain constraints can limit deviation from expected neutrino behavior to below $10^{-3}$, exceeding current limits on a similar problem related to other subatomic particles. However, if we consider only certain other constraints, large unitarity violations can occur and be confirmed or disproven with the currently operating FASER$\nu$ experiment in a significant margin of error.

This research develops an innovative method for solving the containment problem with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents. The new algorithm is a modification of the existing Brzozowski's algorithm for regular expression synthesis, with a complementary component to handle containment queries. It offers efficient containment checks, combining well-known properties of Brzozowski's algorithm with a complementary component that ensures correctness and a fixed character set, enabling decentralized computation. A supporting tool, developed during this research, is a Python module called erei, providing a command-line interface for solving containment queries and character set problems with regular expressions and user-defined character sets.

Our proposed EMA-VIO model employs a dual external memory architecture for visual-inertial optimization, enabling efficient navigation by allocating memory for state prediction and correction. By leveraging memory allocation, the model minimizes unnecessary computations associated with massive memory updates, thereby achieving significant performance improvements. In experiments, our model demonstrates superior performance in traditional benchmark tasks and exceptional robustness in challenging scenarios due to its effective rejection of excessive memory updates. Furthermore, results show that the model's performance is on par with that of state-of-the-art method VIO-DS, but with a computational efficiency that is nearly 2 times better.

We develop a theoretical framework that extends the Weyl semimetal theory to higher orders, specifically focusing on the third-order term in a three-dimensional system with time-reversal symmetry. Our model incorporates a novel "square-root" term and demonstrates its stability through a detailed expansion of the Fermi arc spectrum. Furthermore, we predict that a particular momentum characteristic, resulting from the interaction of second-order touches, exhibits a unique "four-fold" closure and related anomalous transport phenomena. Our proposed model also offers possible experimental signatures for detecting the square-root term by analyzing the Berry curvature flux and the resulting anomalous Hall effect.

This project investigates the numerical solution to a fundamental problem in inverse problems and image processing, which involves recovering a missing portion of a conductivity map based on boundary voltage measurements, using a simplified Maxwell's equations model. A non-iterative finite element method is developed for this problem in a restricted class of piecewise constant conductivities. The method first establishes a stable and optimal convergence rate for the simplified Maxwell's equations before deriving a stable and optimal convergence rate for the original problem. This approach yields a robust and high-performance solution for this problem. To facilitate implementation, a practical algorithm based on the stable finite element method is provided. Notably, this project is the first to establish a stable and optimal convergence rate for the original Maxwell's equations based on a non-iterative approach.

This paper delves into the properties and characteristics of a series of vertex operator algebras based on the parafermion mode, as initially proposed in the paper titled "A Series of Vertex Operator Algebras Associated with Long Orthosymplective Lie Supalgebras" by Y.-H. Wang and the second author. It expands on the previous work by providing the underlying generator set for these algebras and verifying the satisfaction of the graded Lie algebra property for the associated Lie algebras. Moreover, it establishes the connection between these vertex operator algebras and the W-algebras based on the simple Lie algebras $osp(1|2n)$, as well as determining the central charge of the W-algebras. Finally, it presents two-unitary matrix representations of these vertex operator algebras.

This paper introduces the Federated Selective Integration (FeSI) approach for a distributed knowledge fusion framework. In large-scale networks, FeSI enables the collaborative creation of high-quality knowledge bases while addressing the challenge of low-quality data. The proposed approach combines two key components: a matching algorithm and a integration algorithm. The matching algorithm identifies compatible knowledge pairs across the network, whereas the integration algorithm is responsible for combining selected pairs into a unified knowledge base. Our research is exemplified through the implementation of Human Daily Activities (HDAs) a domain with limited and disparate annotated data available across the network. Comparative evaluations of FeSI with alternative methods, including centralised and distributed approaches, reveal a significant improvement in performance metrics such as precision, recall and ATEC.

This study explores how environmental dimensionality and the location of head
coordinates influence a neuron's response characteristics within the entorhinal
cortex. We utilize a linear non-parametric model to analyze place cells located
within the medial entorhinal cortex. Our results indicate that certain patterns
emerge across a wide range of scaling factors, supporting the idea that the
entorhinal cortex's grid neuron pattern is consistent across different spatial
scales. Additionally, our findings reveal how the orientation of the head
coordinates and the dimensionality of the environment impact a neuron's
response. We discover that certain neurons are affected by the head coordinates'
orientation, while others are influenced by the spatial dimensionality. We
also find evidence suggesting the head coordinates' orientation has a unique
impact on the neuron's response and that this impact cannot be captured by
considering the grid neuron pattern alone. We believe our results have implicit
policy-based underlying mechanisms and that our findings are relevant to other
place cells located within the hippocampus.

Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may influence the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by their rotation rates.

Our research reveals that magnetically active stars exhibit greater activity levels when comparing their surface flux to slow and fast rotators. It also indicates that magnetically active stars maintain similar activity levels when comparing their surface flux to solar-type rapid rotators. It is suspected that anti-solar differential rotation may instead mirror the characteristics of slow rotators.

We explore how magnetic cycles might operate in slowly rotating stars through an analytic model, assuming that they involve a combination of alpha-effect generation of magnetic field and turbulent dissipation. It predicts that these stars' magnetic activity should correlate with their rotational velocity, specifically displaying an inverse relationship.

We provide a theoretical framework to determine the rank of elliptic curves in quartic extensions of the rationals, specifically focusing on cases involving the symmetric and alternating groups, and we apply this framework to a substantial number of elliptic curves, ultimately determining the rank for the majority of them. Additionally, our results involve establishing infinite families of elliptic curves with the largest possible rank, i.e., rank 4, in both $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions of the rationals.

A crucial aspect of quantum field theory's complexity is understood through its connection to thermodynamic parameters in a state known as thermal equilibrium. Complexities are, however, observed to fluctuate greatly depending on the model in question, and there is currently no overarching theory unifying them. A key challenge in studying the quantum conformal field theories (QFCs) is represented by the absence of a clear, all-encompassing picture of entropy generation in these theories. The story changes with the arrival of the quantum null energy condition at the edge (QNEC), which allows the entropy change in any cross-section to be determined using the derivative of the logarithm of the partition function of the theory with respect to a specific variable. By using the QNEC, the speed limit of entropy generation in one-dimensional spaces can be derived as $\Delta S/\Delta \alpha=1/2$, and this result is shown to hold for all quasi-local regions, and for both spatial and temporal sections. Furthermore, the QNEC can be employed to define four distinct entropy generation rates for regions with specific shapes, such as a sphere, and the corresponding rates are derived for them. The fluctuation rate is found to reach the maximal possible rate of entropy generation/decay, given by $\Delta S/\Delta \alpha=2$, and the same result is obtained for the entropy generation rate in the development of the entanglement gap, and for the rate of entropy generation in two-dimensional spaces. We investigate the real-time identifiability of quantum states under single-shot measurements in the Bloch ball. Depending on the asymmetry of the state, different types of measurement are either effectively identifying the state in a finite time or the time approaches infinity. Also, we find that in the asymptotic limit, certain classes of measurement that are increasingly sensitive as they approach a certain point in the Bloch ball are optimal for state identification. Additionally, we find the minimum time required for some classes of pure states to be identified with a specific type of measurement.

This paper introduces an innovative approach to deriving upper bounds for the norm of a specific interpolation operator. Specifically, we establish explicit upper bounds for the norm of a operator that maps functions from L^1(-1,1) to the normed space C^0(-1,1), utilizing an operator-known-to-exist theorem. We also provide a novel method for determining upper bounds for the norm of an interpolation operator inspired by the method of B. Sz.-Nagy.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in metal resonators, enabling the identification of coupling between superconducting circuits and residual charge carriers. Utilizing a gauge invariant approach, we determine the local magnetic field strength and demonstrate its relationship to the local dielectric characteristics. Our findings reveal that carrier concentrations can be controlled during fabrication or modified through light exposure. We also find that ferroelectric impurities have a negligible influence but that metal flakes contribute to decoherence. This research highlights the computational capability to understand and identify local phenomena in complex systems and suggests that light-induced effects could serve as a means to reduce decoherence in quantum devices.

This study offers a motivic interpretation of curved K-theory for certain algebraic varieties, specifically utilizing a relative version of motivic spectral sequence and identifying a pattern that reflects the geometric properties of these varieties. Our analysis indicates that the motivic curved K-theory spectrum for these varieties is directly connected to the geometric properties, specifically showing that it bridges the difference between the algebraic and geometric versions of these varieties. Our work also establishes a link between the motivic and classical versions of these types of spaces, specifically demonstrating that the motivic curved K-theory spectrum is equivalent to the classical curved K-theory spectrum when looking at these varieties through a specific type of space that is based on fields with a specific characteristic.

Our atmosphere has not reached stability yet, largely due to a lack of strong internal heat and dynamo activity within our core. This absence prevents the geodynamo and solar wind from shielding our atmosphere from cometary and coronal mass cargos. As a result, atmospheric gases, such as oxygen and hydrogen, are lost over time. In the case of Venus, which has a much stronger internal heat source, this process has been slower. We propose that this has allowed Venus to retain a substantial amount of atmospheric gas rich in carbon dioxide, which in turn has prevented water from being broken down completely and led to a continued cycle of gas exchange. This cycle has significant implications for the planets' atmospheric evolution, suggesting that the need for rapid generation of core momentum is a misconception. Instead, a strong internal heat source can enable planets to withstand the effects of cometary and solar impacts, maintaining variable isocarbonate levels in their atmospheres.

Investigating the interactions between ions and molecules in a quantum system in motion is highly challenging. To address this, we've developed a novel reaction nanoscopy technique that utilizes vacuum ultraviolet light to instantly break up nanoscale droplets of glycol into small groups of ions and molecules while we observe the reaction. By employing this method, we've studied the dynamics of these droplets and found that they've entered a state of quantum coherence. Through further analysis, we've derived a new method for detecting, interfering with, and observing the motion of ions within these droplets. Additionally, our technique has enabled us to study the quantum vacuum better, as it allows us for the first time to directly measure the expected effects of particle pair creation on the motion of ions.

Recent breakthroughs in the evaluation of quantum circuit complexity via matrix product state representations can be build upon to create a practical framework for breaking down these states into elementary quantum gates within popular circuits such as the holographic Hamiltonian and tensor network codes like CSS codes for quantum error correction. This framework involves applying a systematic decomposition process to MPSThe decomposition process involves applying a systematic decomposition process to MPS into a quantum circuit consisting of a limited set of unitary operations, which can then be mapped to a corresponding classical circuit. This leads to a more manageable calculation of circuit complexity and specific code properties. Our research focuses on an efficient decomposition of MPS into a minimal quantum circuit, which we demonstrate through a straightforward application of the decomposition process to notable examples, including the holographic Hamiltonian and various quantum codes, particularly the 2D toric code, stabilizer codes, and the Haah enzyme code. These decompositions, displayed on our website under the category of quantum circuit decomposition, showcase the practical utility of this framework, showcasing which regions of an MPS exhibit highly complex unitary transformations when decomposed.

The success of cancer treatment significantly depends on the accuracy of tumor diagnosis, which often involves time-consuming and labor-intensive processes powered by advancements in computational technologies. Computer vision experts have been working to incorporate artificial intelligence into digital pathology, with many achieving impressive results in classifying biopsy images. However, they often forget that biopsy samples represent just a small part of larger tissues, which are part of organs, and that tumors often develop at various locations within cancers. In an effort to bypass this limitation, researchers have been attempting to construct a unified representation of tissues by combining the information contained in multiple biopsy samples. Yet, as structural systems, tissues have distinct levels of organization, from the fine details of cell nuclei up to broader patterns. Therefore, building a unified tissue representation necessitates organizing the network at different levels of hierarchy. With this context in mind, we propose a novel approach that not only combines the information in biopsy samples but also captures the complex hierarchy present in tissues. Our method enables the creation of a unified representation of tissues by defining a new multi-scale learning objective that integrates the information in biopsy samples and incorporates a top-down mechanism that helps the model focus on detecting objects at different levels of abstraction. To test our approach, we developed a large-scale cancer dataset consisting of over 20 billion pixels and containing over 100,000 cell nuclei across multiple tissue samples, which we used to evaluate the performance of our method on the classification of biopsy images. Point processes that exhibit nonlinear dependencies pose significant
challenge in modeling real-world phenomena. Real-time, adaptive methods to
analyze these point processes are particularly crucial. In this paper, we develop
a real-time estimation framework for a specific type of non-linear point
process, the Hawkes process, using a nonlinear function that can be tailored
to fit specific data characteristics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this
approach by applying it to the analysis of a real-world network data set,
showing that it is more sensitive than traditional methods in identifying
hidden connections. Additionally, we find that it successfully captures the
temporal characteristics of various data sets, including the arrival rates of
earthquake and terrorist event data. Furthermore, we discover that there is
a significant difference in the estimator and the true arrival rates as the
sampling frequency increases.

This research extends the application of the Rapid Multipole Method to solve partial differential equations, specifically demonstrating its efficacy on a complex problem involving the simulation of fluid dynamics with rotating objects in a variety of scenarios.

Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have reached optimal performance in medical image segmentation, the process is hindered by a large number of required annotations for training. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques have potential in decreasing this burden, but they are hindered when datasets are small and have few labeled images. One method to enhance performance involves leveraging existing annotated datasets of similar anatomical structures for training. Nevertheless, a challenge arises when adapting the model to cross-domain segmentation, primarily because the target and source domains have distinct image appearances. In this paper, we introduce an innovative SSL framework that combines contrastive learning and SSL techniques to accomplish cross-domain adaptation for segmentation across comparable anatomical structures. The model employs a learning strategy that treats annotations from the target domain as virtual pseudo-targets and the source domain as a target itself, using a contrastive loss function to achieve adaptation. Additionally, we propose using a contrastive loss function to encourage the model to distinguish between authentic and pseudo-target annotations from the target domain. The framework is versatile and may be applied to various anatomical structures and medical datasets. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework on the segmentation of comparable structures in cardiac and brain datasets, particularly in scenarios where the target domain has limited labeled images.

The foundation of contemporary supergravity, often referred to as the '1.5 order trick', has been extensively analyzed in a simplified theoretical framework based on the Wess-Zumino theory. A straightforward examination indicates that this 1.5 order formalism is inherently defective in all contexts. Although it appears that the associated algebra is closed, a detailed examination in a simplified setting reveals the presence of a non-nilpotent BRS operator generated at the 1.5 order level, which significantly complicates efforts to construct a precise nilpotent operator. All attempts to generate a valid nilpotent algebra at the 1.5 order level have been unsuccessful in this analysis. Nevertheless, it is possible to generate a valid nilpotent algebra at the 3rd order of expansion. A key aspect of the associated superfield transformations is the incorporation of auxiliary fields, which are intimately connected with the generation of a nilpotent 3rd order algebra. In contrast, the 1.5 order formalism fails to adequately account for these fields within the superfield framework. A plausible explanation for the apparent success in other approaches may involve the presence of external supertransformations, which complicate the analysis and mask the presence of a defective 1.5 order formalism.

The introduction of a high-power laser into a specific type of magnetized plasma can lead to a unique phenomenon known as polarization alteration. Research has shown that this phenomenon results in a significant increase in pulse energy when a linearly polarized laser interacts with a non-homogeneous magnetic field. However, the required strong magnetic field poses a challenge in creating such conditions in a laboratory setting. To address this limitation, we propose using a much weaker magnetic field that is achieved through the creation of a nonlinear ion density profile. It has been found that this approach can also lead to a significant increase in pulse energy under specific theoretical conditions. Nevertheless, achieving these conditions in an actual experiment remains a challenge. To address this, we need to re-examine the requirements for the highest possible energy amplification, which can be achieved when the magnetic field is high enough to break down the laser pulse into multiple components, ultimately resulting in a significant increase in pulse energy. A model that explains how the spectral component of the plasma affects energy amplification is also presented in this discussion.

The tau lepton's electric dipole moment (EDM) is examined within a framework that incorporates perturbative QCD at a scale of 2 GeV, with the goal of better understanding this quantity's behavior. By exploring the impact of condensates within the operator product expansion, the underlying system's renormalized parameters are revealed. The EDM is found to be linked to the value of the QCD phase shift, as expressed through the imaginary part of the chromoelectric self-energy of the quark. A previously unexplored region of parameter space is identified for the EDM, which may be probed by the CDF II experiment at the Tevatron or the NA62 experiment at CERN.

The rank metric, employed in certain code-based cryptography systems to prevent the improper use of encrypted data, can lead to errors in decoding encrypted messages. Unfortunately, current decoding techniques in these systems typically fall short of achieving optimal error correction and often result in the transmission of incorrect data to the intended recipient. A recently developed hybrid decoding approach has shown improvement over these conventional methods, but it comes with a significant disadvantage of its own - it requires a substantial amount of previously decoded message data. In this research, a new decoding strategy is presented that not only outperforms the hybrid approach but also avoids the need for prior message data, making it a more practical solution for real-world applications.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we examine a specific four-point function in CFT$_2$, specifically involving spinning operators and conformal primary fields. Focusing on the AdS$_2$ segment of these four-point functions, we establish an explicit transformation under the symplectic symmetry group $\mathrm{Sp}(4)$. Furthermore, we establish a direct relationship between these four-point functions and the AdS$_2$ segment of conformal block calculations in CFT$_2$. Additionally, we detail a systematic approach for the spin decomposition of conformal block calculations in CFT$_2$. This involves introducing a specific parametrization for the conformal block, establishing a direct relationship between the spinning conformal block and the spinning AdS$_2$ segment of a four-point function, and subsequently deriving the spin decomposition through the study of $\mathrm{Sp}(4)$ symmetries.

Future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background will be able to measure a crucial parameter $r$ with high precision, however a significant challenge lies ahead. Delensing, the process to extract a primordial signal buried under another signal caused by gravitational lensing, is key. To improve this process beyond traditional quadratic estimators which may not be sufficient, the next generation experiments could potentially benefit from more sophisticated methods such as a maximum a posteriori estimator or even a machine learning approach, the neural network, that was previously shown to have superior lensing reconstruction performance when compared to the quadratic estimator in certain scenarios. We take this further by investigating these methods' performance when removing a significant amount of noise to simulate a primordial signal. We discover that the neural network estimator's delensing performance is on par with the iterative estimator, the benchmark in our field. We found that in order for these methods to work properly it is necessary to train the model under controlled conditions. We then extend these training techniques to models that account for foreground contamination, the complexity of which often exceeds our ability to simulate their effects.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a precise relationship between characteristic classes from differential geometry and polynomial invariants from commutative algebra, specifically regarding the Pontrjagin classes of a manifold. This discovery led to the creation of the geometric combinatorics branch within the Department of Mathematics at Purdue University. Nearly two decades later, in 2009, Jozsa and the author were tasked with verifying the general extension of their method to computationally determine various characteristic classes of a manifold, using geometric techniques. This involvement sparked new insights into the original Gelfand-MacPherson approach. As a result, an alternative explanatory diagram was devised and is now made publicly available for the first time.

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for Type II supernovae with short plateau phases.

To greatly decrease the number of images required in optical lobster-eye lenses' detection of pulsating X-ray sources, we propose using these lenses in a multiplexed configuration, utilizing the inherent periodic structure of the lenses to achieve this reduction. This optical lobster-eye lens arrangement can be very effective at detecting short-term changes in pulsating X-rays and could potentially be applied to a large field of view X-ray monitoring system.

We establish a simplified, set-theoretic version of the concept of partial uniform ellipticity for differential operators. Furthermore, this leads to a more accessible proof of the continuous extension property for functions on sets with limited structure, specifically focusing on the underlying theory of partial uniform ellipticity.

To investigate the role of velocity field in forming dark matter halos, a deep learning framework was used to create predictive models for the distribution of dark matter particles within halos. The model was trained on a simulation dataset consisting of position and velocity information for dark matter particles, allowing it to estimate the weight function that governs the distribution of particles within halos. The results showed that when velocity information was included, the weight function separated into two distinct components: one related to the position field and and independent component. The position-dependent part of the weight function was found to match previous findings, while the independent component represented a secondary distribution of particles within halos. It was found that velocity field plays a significant role in contributing to the weight function and is essential for predicting the particle distribution within halos.

Music transcription, specifically piano transcription, is a complex task with numerous applications, notably in music education and entertainment. What sets it apart from other transcription tasks is the need to capture dynamic relationships in audio data, which comprises time-stamp information. This paper introduces a semi-supervised technique using low-rank matrix factorization to analyze acoustic data combined with musical notes, with the aim of transcribing piano audio with minimal human input. Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization, an extension of NMF, is a suitable method for this challenge due to its capacity for temporal analysis and feature extraction. Our novel approach builds upon this technique by incorporating note labels as additional columns in the data matrix, allowing for the inclusion of limited annotated data to inform the factorization process. This results in a complex optimization problem, which we solve using an iterative algorithm that takes advantage of the convexity of the NMF objective function. Our method was tested on the MAPS dataset with promising outcomes, demonstrating its potential as a piano transcription tool.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium in rotating stars under the principles of special relativity. Our method, tailored for adiabatic indices $\Gamma \geq 4/3$, was successfully tested against established solutions, including both slow and rapid rotations. Notably, our scheme allows for the inclusion of surface magnetic fields within the equilibrium configurations, a feature absent in current general-relativistic numerical models of rotating stars.

A critical challenge in creating machine learning models for extracting data from documents lies in their extensive reliance on manually labeled examples by experts. Unfortunately, this process proves costly and labor-intensive. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a pioneering alternative to extensive labeling sessions by combining two cutting-edge techniques: active learning and task-oriented semantic role labeling, which significantly reduces labeling expenses without compromising the accuracy of the models. Our method allows the system to focus on highly informative samples for labeling and utilize a pre-trained model to interpret documents with ease. Through testing on real-world data, our approach demonstrates a notable reduction in labeling costs of up to $5 in comparison to traditional methods.

The detection of gravitational waves by laser interferometers like LIGO and Virgo opens up new possibilities for researching the universe through waveform patterns produced by mergers of non-compact objects, such as neutron stars and black holes. However, accurately modeling these waveforms using theoretical formulas is extremely challenging due to the need to account for numerous variables, including masses, spins, and the geometry of the binary system. A new approach, using artificial intelligence techniques to classify waveforms based on their content, has been developed and put through its paces in a simulated environment. The study employed a neural network to classify waveforms as either observable or unobservable by current detectors, and to categorize them into five distinct mass configurations; it also involved over 1,000 generated waveforms. The findings show that the network's performance is highly reliable, with an error rate of less than 0.05%, when distinguishing between observable and unobservable waveforms. When it comes to assigning mass classifications, the network's accuracy ranges from 75% to over 99%, varying depending on the specific configuration.

The significant disparity in healthcare outcomes beyond just medical factors necessitates the incorporation of social determinants of wellness into care delivery. However, identifying these determinants poses a significant challenge in machine learning (ML) due to the diversity of data presented in clinical notes, requiring a pioneering approach. We introduce an innovative method using a unique neural network, where a marker-driven team is tasked with efficiently extracting relevant information from clinical notes, generating a more accurate and comprehensive social determinants dataset. This technique is part of a broader project aiming to integrate social determinants into an existing HIPAA-compliant NLP pipeline. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method through a dataset expansion experiment, where we successfully boost the SDOI code coverage by over 8-fold after applying our system. The development and training of this marker-driven network are detailed in our methodology section, while the results and a discussion of the findings are presented in the outcome section.

Some swimming animals like scallops employ a gait where they alternate forward and backward movements, maintaining a fixed angle between their bodies. This gait generates optimal speed and efficiency if certain conditions are met. In our research, we address two key queries regarding this swimming pattern. First, we determine the optimal speed and efficiency when there are no obstacles in the path. This involves solving a linear quadratic optimal control problem. We also find the optimal angle between the animal's body and its direction of motion under these conditions. Additionally, we investigate how this swimming pattern performs in the presence of external forcing and flow. This includes analyzing the stability of the system and identifying the fastest and most efficient speeds.

The COVID-19 pandemic forced widespread remote work, leading to a sudden shift in urban interactions. This change created an opportunity to examine how people's behaviors adjusted and how these adjustments affected the income disparity of urban interactions. Through a statistical analysis of 2 million anonymized trips collected from a leading mobility service provider, we found that pandemic-related remote work accelerated the income disparity of urban interactions. Before the pandemic, the income disparity of urban interactions followed a steady decline, but this trend reversed after the pandemic with a significant widening of the disparity. A statistical model revealed that pandemic-related remote work and its associated behavioral shifts were the primary factors contributing to the increased disparity. It was observed that workers who remained employed and interacted with urban areas after the pandemic significantly differed in their trip generation patterns compared to those who lost their jobs. They spent a smaller proportion of their daily urban interaction time visiting recreational areas and a larger proportion visiting food and drink establishments. The trip generation model identified various urban features that attracted low-income and high-income trippers at significantly different rates. For instance, low-income trippers were drawn to recreational areas, homeless shelters, and public transportation hubs, whereas high-income trippers were attracted to cultural institutions, restaurants, and high-end retail stores. Understanding how pandemic-related remote work and resulting behavioral shifts affected urban interactions trippers can be applied to inform policymakers, urban planners, and businesses in the aftermath of global disruptions.

The massive protostar 50 km away from the center of the star-forming region OMC1 has been accumulating material at a slow pace for approximately 500,000 years. Despite its size, it lacks a sustained burst of growth that typically occurs around this stage of development. By analyzing observations of radio waves from a nearby molecular cloud using a technique called radiative transfer, scientists discovered that a combination of the protostar's own energy and extreme solar winds from nearby large stars are preventing material from accumulating freely. This blockade is also responsible for shaping the shape of the surrounding gas into a distinctive horseshoe shape. Additionally, scientists believe that episodes of solar winds may be causing ripples in the gas accumulation around the protostar, potentially creating opportunities for it to grow at a faster rate.

Buchholz established a meaningful way to measure the local distinguishability of states within a given state space. This measurement serves as the foundation for evaluating the interpretability of quantum field theories. Building upon Buchholz's approach, a method was developed to determine the distinguishability of states by using wedge-local networks of observables. This development involved using Longo-Witten endomorphisms to expand the state space while maintaining wedge-local properties. A key finding was that a state space is fully interpretable if its associated algebra can be realized as a soft wedge of a larger algebra, itself derived from a extension of the Longo-Witten category that includes category $\cal N$ interventions.
